title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
extended_summary:
This conceptual paper addresses the growing need for teachers to develop artificial intelligence (AI) digital competencies as AI-based educational tools become more common in post-pandemic online and blended learning. The authors argue that while AI can support personalized learning, automated feedback, learning analytics, and efficiency in teaching and assessment, many teachers lack the technical, pedagogical, and ethical knowledge needed to use these tools well.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, the paper synthesizes existing literature and examples to identify the opportunities and challenges of AI in education and to specify the competencies teachers need. It revisits and adapts two established frameworks: the European DigCompEdu framework and the P21 framework for twenty-first century learning. The paper also references broader AI competency models and a revised TPACK perspective to argue that teacher AI competence should include both technical and non-technical dimensions.

The intended population is educators, especially teachers and school leaders working in AI-enabled educational environments, with examples drawn broadly from online, blended, and higher-education contexts as well as K-12-related AI literacy discussions. The main conclusion is that teacher preparation should move beyond basic technical skills toward a holistic set of AI competencies spanning professional engagement, instructional design, content choices across disciplines, and student learning competencies, including ethics, collaboration, creativity, and responsible AI use.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework paper rather than an empirical evaluation study. It synthesizes prior literature and proposes adaptations of competency frameworks, but does not present a clear study design, sample, or causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct intervention effects were measured, so there is no estimable impact on student outcomes or institutional outcomes. The paper is useful for framing expectations and competencies, but it does not demonstrate measurable K-12 impact.
